Blossom
blŏs´um
n., v. (a flower, to bloom; rendering Hebrew tsuts and perach)
Old English blostm, a flower. Blossom is the stage of promise — the visible pledge of fruit not yet formed.

Biblical Definition

To blossom is to break into flower. Aaron's rod settles a rebellion by doing it overnight: “the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds” (Num 17:8) — bud, blossom, and ripe fruit at once on dead wood. Isaiah promises that “the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose” (Isa 35:1), and Habakkuk sets his famous confession against its failure: “although the fig tree shall not blossom… yet I will rejoice in the LORD” (Hab 3:17–18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines blossom as the flower of a plant, or the essential organs of fructification; and as a verb, to put forth blossoms or flowers, to bloom, to flower.

expand to see more

BLOSSOM, n. The flower of a plant, or the essential organs of reproduction, with their appendages.

BLOSSOM, v.i. To put forth blossoms or flowers; to bloom; to blow; to flower.

2. To flourish and prosper.

Key Scripture

Num 17:8 — "And it came to pass, that on the morrow Moses went into the tabernacle of witness; and, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds."

Isa 35:1 — "The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose."

Hab 3:17 — "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:"

Hab 3:18 — "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation."

Modern Corruption

Faith is measured by visible flourishing, so a barren season is read as divine displeasure — and Habakkuk's whole point is that worship survives the empty branch.

expand to see more

Numbers 17 is a lesson about how God settles disputes over authority. Twelve rods were laid up before the LORD overnight, and one came out carrying buds, blossoms, and ripe almonds together — three stages at once on wood that had been cut from the tree. The vindication was not an argument but a resurrection, and the rod was kept in the ark as a permanent answer to the murmurers.

Habakkuk 3 supplies the harder lesson. Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat… yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The prophet lists total agricultural collapse — every source of food gone — and then places his joy somewhere the failure cannot reach. Blossom or no blossom, the object of his rejoicing is unchanged.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsuts (H6692), to blossom or flourish; perach (H6525), a bud or flower; both used of Aaron's rod in Numbers 17.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsuts (H6692) — to blossom, flourish; Numbers 17:8, Psalm 92:7, the wicked spring as the grass.

Hebrew perach (H6525) — bud, blossom; the almond blossoms of the golden candlestick, Exodus 25:33.

Hebrew parach (H6524) — to bud, break forth; Isaiah 35:1-2, it shall blossom abundantly.

Usage

"“Bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds” — three stages at once on dead wood."

"“The desert… shall blossom as the rose” — the promise to barren ground."

"“Although the fig tree shall not blossom… yet I will rejoice” — worship past the empty branch."
